title: Rent on Money
intro: Grace & Co. opens its first bank account. Money, it turns out, has a price.

blocks.html:
Think about renting a house.

You do not own it. Somebody else does.

They let you use it, and you pay them for the privilege. That payment is called rent.

Money works exactly the same way.

If you use somebody else's money, you pay them rent for it.

That rent has a different name. It is called interest.

Interest is rent on money.

Two things decide how much rent you pay.

The first is the amount of money.

The second is the rate — a percentage, for each year you keep it.

And here is the part most people never think about.

It runs in both directions.

When you put money in a bank, the bank is borrowing it from you.

So the bank pays you rent.

Every percentage gear you own already works on this. Nothing new to learn. Only a new name for it.

blocks.prompt: Grace & Co. puts £200 into a savings account. The bank pays 10% a year.
blocks.hint: The bank is renting your £200. The rent is 10% of it. Your 10% gear: divide by 10.

parts.label: Interest the bank pays you after year 1 (£)
parts._working: 10% of £200. Her 10% gear is divide by 10: 200 ÷ 10 = £20. Deliberately the easiest gear she owns, as the early win.

parts.label: Total in the account after year 1 (£)
parts._working: The original £200 is still hers, and the £20 of interest is added on top: 200 + 20 = £220. Establishes the shape 'amount plus interest', which is what next session compounds.

blocks.prompt: A different bank, a different rate. This one holds £300 and pays 5% a year.
blocks.hint: Find 10% first, then halve it — that is your 5% gear from Unit 1.

parts.label: Interest the bank pays you after year 1 (£)
parts._working: 5% of £300. Her halving gear: 10% of 300 = £30, half of that = £15.

parts.label: Total in the account after year 1 (£)

blocks.html:
Go back to that first account.

You saved £200 at 10%. The bank paid you £20.

That £20 felt good. It was income.

Now turn the desk around.

Imagine you borrow £200 from the bank instead, at the same 10%.

Now you are the one using somebody else's money.

So you pay the rent. You pay the bank £20.

Look carefully at what changed.

The amount did not change. Still £200.

The rate did not change. Still 10%.

The interest did not change. Still £20.

The only thing that changed is which side of the desk you sit on.

That is the whole of banking in one sentence.

An analyst never asks whether interest is good or bad. An analyst asks: am I the saver here, or the borrower?

blocks.prompt: Now you are the borrower. Grace & Co. borrows £400 to buy a lemonade cart. The rate is 25% a year.
blocks.hint: 25% is a quarter. Halve it, then halve it again — your quarter gear. Then remember you still owe the £400 itself.

parts.label: Interest you pay after year 1 (£)
parts._working: 25% of £400. Her double-halving gear from w1s2: half of 400 is 200, half again is £100.

parts.label: Total you must hand back after year 1 (£)
parts._working: The borrowed £400 plus £100 of rent on it: 400 + 100 = £500. Worth her noticing that a quarter-rate means paying back five pounds for every four borrowed.

blocks.html:
One small word in that rate is doing a lot of work.

The word is year.

25% a year does not mean £100 once and then you are done.

It means £100 of rent for each year you keep the money.

Keep it two years and the bank wants rent twice.

Interest is not a fee. It is rent for time.

So the longer you borrow, the more you pay. And the longer you save, the more you earn.

Hold on to that. It is the whole of the next board meeting.

blocks.prompt:
Boss question. Grace & Co. is doing both at once.

The company has £600 sitting in a savings account, earning 5% a year.

It also has a £200 loan on the cart, costing 20% a year.
 AmountRate each year
Savings account£6005%
Loan on the cart£20020%
You are saving three times as much as you borrowed. So you must be winning. Check it.
blocks.hint: Work out the two rents separately. For the savings, 5% of £600. For the loan, 20% of £200. Then compare the two.

parts.label: Interest the bank pays you after year 1 (£)
Interest you pay on the loan after year 1 (£)
Overall, is Grace & Co. up or down this year? (up or down)
parts._working: Earned £30, paid £40. More rent went out than came in, so the company is £10 DOWN — despite saving three times as much as it borrowed. The lesson: a high rate on a small debt beats a low rate on big savings. This is the same shape as the w2s2 trap, where a big margin on a small business lost to a small margin on a big one. Accept list is wide because 'worse off' and 'losing' are equally right answers.

blocks.prompt:
★ Analyst's question. This time you are told the rent, and you have to work out the rate.

You saved £400 for a year, and the bank paid you £20 of interest.

Your friend saved £200 for a year, and her bank also paid her £20.
 Amount savedInterest after year 1
You£400£20
Your friend£200£20
You both got £20. So which of you has the better bank?
blocks.hint: You did this with margins. Compare the interest to the amount it came from, then turn that into a percentage.

parts.label: Your rate (%)
parts._working: £20 out of £400 = 20/400 = 1/20 = 5%. Gear check: 10% of 400 is 40, so 5% is 20 ✓. Accept carries the decimal twin 0.05 because the engine reads a typed "5%" as 0.05 — without it, a right answer with a % sign marks wrong.

parts.label: Your friend's rate (%)
parts._working: £20 out of £200 = 20/200 = 1/10 = 10%. Decimal twin 0.1 included for the same reason.

parts.label: Better bank? (you or your friend)
parts._working: The friend. Same £20 of rent, but out of half the money, so her rate is twice as good. Exactly the margin move from w2s2 wearing a new costume: the pounds tell you how much, the percentage tells you how good.

blocks.html:
📈 Market story for the dinner table:

Go and look at a real bank.

It will pay you about 2% a year on your savings.

It will charge somebody else about 6% a year on a loan.

It is renting the very same money. Your money, in fact.

So the board question is this: what is the 4% in the middle for?

(You already have the word for that gap. You learned it two meetings ago.)

Think about what a bank has to pay for out of that 4% — buildings, staff, cash machines — and what happens to the money when somebody borrows and never pays it back.

Then the field assignment, analyst. Ask Dad two questions and bring the answers back:

1. What rate does his savings account actually pay?
2. What rate does a credit card charge?

Be ready for the second number to be a lot bigger than you expect.

done.title: Meeting adjourned ✓
done.html:
Interest: rent on money.

You can work out what a saver earns, what a borrower pays, and the rate itself when you are only told the rent.

And you found the trap — a high rate on a small loan can quietly beat a low rate on big savings.

Next: The Snowball — what happens when you leave the money alone for a second year, and the bank starts charging rent on the rent.
